Watch: letter → number → binary

The ASCII table tap a key

A

Codes 0–31 are invisible control characters (like Enter). Capital letters start at 65, lowercase at 97: a difference of 32.

ASCII vs Unicode

ASCIIUnicode
Bits per character7 (stored in 8)8 to 32 (UTF-8 / UTF-16 / UTF-32)
Characters1281,100,000+ possible code points
CoversEnglish letters, digits, symbolsAll world languages, maths, emoji
File sizeSmallerLarger
Text size (bits) = characters × bits per character

“HELLO” in ASCII (8 bits each) = 5 × 8 = 40 bits = 5 bytes

Part 2
Sound:
sample rate & bit depth

 
Watch: from wave to numbers

 

  
Two settings control quality

  
Sample rate
Snapshots taken per second, measured in Hz.
CD audio: 44,100 Hz

  
Bit depth (resolution)
Bits used to store each snapshot.
CD audio: 16 bits = 65,536 levels

  
File size = sample rate × bit depth × seconds × channels

  
Example: 44,100 × 16 × 10 s × 1 = 7,056,000 bits ÷ 8 = 882,000 bytes ≈ 0.88 MB

Part 3
Images:
resolution & colour depth

 
Watch: pixels and bits

 

  
A bitmap is a grid of pixels

  
Resolution
Width × height in pixels. More pixels = more detail and a bigger file.

  
Colour depth
Bits per pixel. 1 bit = 2 colours, 8 bits = 256, 24 bits = 16.7 million.

  
File size (bits) = width × height × colour depth

  
Example: 100 × 100 × 24 = 240,000 bits ÷ 8 = 30,000 bytes ≈ 29.3 KB

Cheat sheet

 
TopicKey ideaBigger number means…

 
ASCII / UnicodeEach character → a binary codeMore characters, larger file

 
Sample rateSamples per second (Hz)Smoother, more accurate sound

 
Bit depthBits per sampleMore volume levels, less “crunch”

 
ResolutionPixels (width × height)More detail

 
Colour depthBits per pixelMore colours

 
8 bits = 1 byte
1 KB = 1024 bytes
Bits ÷ 8 = bytes
